title: Bits, bytes, hex and Base64
summary: Crypto works on bytes, not strings. Move between text, bytes, hex and Base64 without losing anything.

steps.title: Everything is bytes
body: Every crypto API in .NET takes and returns `byte[]` (or `Span<byte>`). A **byte** is 8 bits, a number from 0 to 255. Keys, hashes, nonces and ciphertexts are byte arrays, *not text*.
Text becomes bytes through an **encoding**, almost always UTF-8:

The reverse trip only works for bytes that *were* text. Random bytes (a key, a ciphertext) are usually not valid UTF-8, and `GetString` silently replaces what it cannot read. Never keep ciphertext in a `string` that way: use hex or Base64.

steps.explain: UTF-8 uses one byte for ASCII and more for other characters. `string.Length` counts UTF-16 characters, not bytes, so never use it for buffer sizes.

steps.title: Hex: two characters per byte
body: **Hex** writes each byte as two digits from `0-9a-f`, 4 bits per character. 255 is `ff`, 16 is `10`, 72 is `48`. Step through the loop below to watch one byte split into its high and low halves.
A 32-byte key is 64 hex characters. Hex is easy to read and compare by eye, which is why logs and test vectors use it.

steps.explain: 0 is `00`, 15 is `0f`, 16 is `10`, and 171 is 10 × 16 + 11, which is `ab`. Every byte is always exactly two characters, leading zeros included.

steps.title: Base64: shorter, for transport
body: **Base64** packs 3 bytes into 4 characters (6 bits each) from `A-Z a-z 0-9 + /`, padding the end with `=`. It is about 33% bigger than the raw bytes, against 100% for hex.

**Base64url** swaps `+` and `/` for `-` and `_` and drops the `=` padding, so the result is safe in URLs and file names. JWTs use it. .NET has `Base64Url` in `System.Buffers.Text`, or you can do the three replacements yourself.
Use the format your protocol specifies. Inside your own app, Base64 for storage and hex for logs and tests is a sensible default.

steps.prompt: A 16-byte value (an AES-128 key, for example) is Base64-encoded. What does this print?
steps.explain: 16 bytes is five full groups of 3 (15 bytes, 20 characters) plus one byte left, which becomes 4 more characters with `==` padding: 24.

steps.prompt: Match each representation to what it looks like for the bytes `[251, 255]`.
steps.explain: Base64url only differs from Base64 in two characters and the missing padding, which is exactly what bites people who decode one with the other's decoder.

steps.title: Hex by hand
prompt: Write `string ToHex(byte[] data)` that returns lowercase hex **without** calling `Convert.ToHexString` or `ToHexStringLower`. Each byte is its high 4 bits (`b >> 4`) then its low 4 bits (`b & 0x0F`), each looked up in `"0123456789abcdef"`.
Then write `byte[] FromHex(string hex)` that reverses it (you may use `Convert.ToByte(pair, 16)`). Throw `FormatException` if the length is odd.
solution: if (hex.Length % 2 != 0) throw new FormatException("Hex needs an even number of characters.");
template: Dojo.Eq("leading zeros are kept", "000f10ab", ToHex(new byte[] { 0, 15, 16, 171 }));
Dojo.Eq("every byte value survives a round trip", dojoAll, FromHex(ToHex(dojoAll)));
hints: Look up `digits[b >> 4]` then `digits[b & 0x0F]` for each byte.
For `FromHex`, take two characters at a time: `hex.Substring(i * 2, 2)`.

steps.title: Base64url for tokens
prompt: Write `string ToBase64Url(byte[] data)` and `byte[] FromBase64Url(string s)` using the normal `Convert` Base64 methods plus string fixes:
- encoding: Base64, then `+` becomes `-`, `/` becomes `_`, and trailing `=` are removed.
- decoding: reverse the swaps and add `=` until the length is a multiple of 4.
template: Dojo.Eq("ToBase64Url of \"hi\" has no padding", "aGk", ToBase64Url(new byte[] { 104, 105 }));
Dojo.Eq($"round trip of {dojoN} bytes", dojoData, FromBase64Url(ToBase64Url(dojoData)));
